title: Permissions: who can do what
summary: Read the -rwxr-x--- of ls -l, and change it with chmod without opening everything.

scheme: └─ type: - a file, d a folder, l a link
text: Every file has an owner (a user) and a group (a team of users).
- The first character is the type of the entry.
- The next nine say what each kind of person may do with it.
Three groups of three letters: for the owner, for the group, for everyone else.
- r read, w write, x execute (run). A - means: not allowed.
- Here sam can change the script, the devs team can only read and run it, the others can do nothing.

scheme: on a file         on a folder
r    read what's in it list the names (ls)
w    change it         add, delete, rename inside
text: The same letters mean something else on a folder.
- Deleting a file needs w on the folder, not on the file!
- A folder without x can't be entered, even if you can read its names.

scheme: sam, alex (in devs) and kim run ./deploy.sh
is it the owner, sam?     yes: use rwx
is it in the group devs?  yes: use r-x
text: Linux checks in this order and stops at the first match.
- alex is in devs, so r-x applies: alex can run the script but not change it.
- root, the administrator, skips these checks (to run a file, it still needs an x somewhere).
chmod changes the permissions. With numbers: r is 4, w is 2, x is 1, and you add them up for each group.
- Or with letters: chmod u+x script.sh adds x for the user (the owner).
- Never chmod 777 to make an error go away: everyone could change the file.
